rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of non-elution. The retention window will guide subsequent gradient trimming and selectivity tests.

Injection 1 already achieves the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method while measuring the critical pair's response to slope.
The shorter gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves the critical pair near its resolution limit. Test higher temperature at the same slope to assess whether selectivity permits further acceleration.

Higher temperature improved the critical pair's resolution while preserving separation elsewhere. Shorten the gradient another step to test whether that gain supports a faster method with maximum CRF.

The six-minute gradient was too steep for the critical pair. Lowering phi1 to 0.80 provides an intermediate slope between injections 3 and 4, aiming to restore full resolution with a last peak earlier than injection 3.

Raise the gradient window by 0.05 while keeping its slope unchanged to remove low-organic time. This tests whether retention can be shortened without losing the full resolution achieved in injection 5.

Raise phi0 to shorten retention while holding phi1 fixed, making the gradient slightly shallower. The shallower slope should help protect the critical pair, whose resolution is now only slightly above 1.5.
Continue raising phi0 at fixed phi1 to shorten the run while modestly reducing gradient steepness. Monitor both the early pair for compression and the central critical pair for loss of selectivity.

Raise the starting organic fraction another step and reduce the endpoint to make the slope shallower, aiming to preserve the central pair while shortening retention. The first pair will show whether the starting fraction is becoming too strong.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a much steeper gradient for a faster, alternative separation regime. The central pair may separate again after an elution-order reversal, while 40 C should give the early pair more selectivity than 50 C.

Keep the fast gradient fixed and lower temperature to test selectivity in the compressed central pair. This isolates the temperature response and checks whether the sub-two-minute separation can recover full resolution.

Return to the near-fully-resolved method from injection 9 and lower phi1 one step to reduce gradient steepness. This should improve the central pair while retaining adequate separation of the early peaks.

Test a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to explore a shorter fully resolved window. Lowering temperature should help retain and separate the early peaks, though the central pair's selectivity must be checked.

Use a slope between injections 9 and 12, targeting just enough central-pair resolution with a shorter gradient program. The 0.60 endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient.

Test the fast-gradient regime with a lower starting fraction to increase differential retention of the central pair. A temperature of 30 C balances the improved central selectivity seen at 25 C against the last-pair separation seen at 40 C.

Return to the fully resolved regime with a slightly shallower slope than injection 8. This targets more resolution margin for the central pair while keeping the first peak away from the essentially unretained region.

Raise temperature one step from injection 16 to test whether its resolution margin permits a shorter separation. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature selectivity, particularly for the early pair.

Compare directly with injection 14 to measure temperature selectivity at the fastest fully resolved window. Lower temperature should improve the early pair and will establish how much resolution margin the central pair loses before further window refinement.

Lower the starting fraction and soften the slope to recover the early-pair resolution lost at 55 C while retaining favorable central-pair selectivity. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, limiting the risk of a prolonged hold.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 16 to test the fastest acceptable slope at phi0 = 0.20. This may shorten the last-peak time below injection 14, though the central pair is expected to approach its resolution limit.

The faster slope in injection 20 lost full resolution, so test a shallower gradient for a more robust maximum-CRF method. This should improve the central pair's margin while keeping all six peaks comfortably within ten minutes.

Raise phi0 one step from injection 21 to shorten retention while preserving a shallow slope for the central pair. This tests a compromise between injection 14's speed and injection 21's resolution margin.

Test a five-degree temperature reduction from injection 22 to improve the limiting early pair. The shallower gradient provides central-pair margin, so this may yield a more robust maximum-CRF separation while remaining under four minutes.

Combine injection 21's lower starting fraction with the temperature that improved early-pair separation in injection 23. This targets stronger resolution margins at maximum CRF, with all peaks still expected well before ten minutes.

Use the final injection to shorten injection 24's separation by increasing the endpoint one step. Its central-pair margin suggests this can preserve maximum CRF, while 45 C protects the early pair; injection 14 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
